extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; scholars studying Hobbes' Leviathan; law and ethics students
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and extraction of Hobbes' statements of the laws of nature, rules governing covenants/contracts, and definitions of justice and related concepts from Leviathan. Useful for interpreting normative principles about obligation, oath, and property in the state of nature and commonwealth contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Rule of Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A general Rule, found out by Reason, by which a man is forbidden to do that which is destructive of his life, or taketh away the means of preserving the same; and to omit that, by which he thinketh it may be best preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes RIGHT (liberty to do or forbear) from LAW (which determines and binds to one of them). Law and Right differ as much as Obligation and Liberty; they are inconsistent when applied to the same matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Right to Everything in the State of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the condition of Man in the state of nature is a condition of warre of every one against every one, every man is governed by his own Reason and has a Right to every thing, even to one another's body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As long as this natural right endures there can be no security of living out the natural allotment of life; lack of common power leads to universal insecurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Law of Nature: Seek Peace
rubrics_metrics.description: A precept of Reason: 'That every man ought to endeavour Peace, as farre as he has hope of obtaining it; and when he cannot obtain it, that he may seek, and use, all helps, and advantages of Warre.' The first branch is the fundamental law of nature: 'To seek Peace, and follow it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second branch (sum of the Right of Nature) is: 'By all means we can, to defend ourselves.' Peace is the primary aim; defence is permitted when peace cannot be secured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Law of Nature: Mutual Transfer of Rights for Peace
rubrics_metrics.description: A man should be willing, when others are so too, to lay down his right to all things (so far as necessary for peace and defence) and be content with so much liberty against other men as he would allow other men against himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is essentially the Golden Rule: mutual renunciation of some natural rights creates the possibility of peace. If others will not lay down rights, there is no reason for an individual to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: What it is to Lay Down a Right
rubrics_metrics.description: To lay down a man's Right is to divest himself of the liberty of hindering another of the benefit of his own right to the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renouncing or passing away a Right does not give a new Right to another (there was nothing beyond original natural rights), but removes impediments so one can enjoy his original right without hindrance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renouncing vs Transferring Right; Obligation and Duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Right is laid aside either by simply renouncing it (not caring who benefits) or by transferring it to another (intending benefit to specific person(s)). After such abandonment or grant, one is OBLIGED not to hinder those to whom the right was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The declarations or signs (words/actions) by which one renounces/ transfers are bonds; their strength comes not from nature but from fear of consequences. Hindrance of a voluntarily given right is INJUSTICE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not All Rights Are Alienable
rubrics_metrics.description: Some rights cannot be understood to have been abandoned or transferred by words or signs — e.g., the right to resist those who assault him to take his life, or to resist being wounded, chained, or imprisoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are rights that cannot be laid down because doing so would not aim at any good for oneself, and because one cannot know the assailant's intent; words suggesting abandonment of such ends are not to be understood as effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract: Mutual Transferring of Right
rubrics_metrics.description: The mutual transferring of Right is that which men call CONTRACT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes transfer of right from delivery of the thing; the thing may be delivered with or after transfer. Contracts involve mutual exchange of rights or promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenant: Promise and Keeping of Faith
rubrics_metrics.description: When one contractor delivers his part now and leaves the other to perform later, that is PACT or COVENANT; one who is to perform later being trusted, his performance is called Keeping Of Promise or Faith; failing (if voluntary) is Violation Of Faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covenant implies trust in future performance; failure of trust (without coercive power) makes such covenants insecure in the state of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-gift vs Contract
rubrics_metrics.description: If transfer is not mutual but one party transfers hoping for friendship, service, reputation, pity, or heavenly reward, it is a GIFT, FREEGIFT, GRACE — essentially voluntary and not a contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gifts aim at the giver's own good (reputation, reciprocity). Distinction affects whether breach counts as injustice (grace vs obligation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of Contract — Express
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs of Contract are either express or by inference. Express signs are words spoken with understanding — of present or past time (e.g., 'I give', 'I have given') or future ('I will give', 'I will grant' — promises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words of present/past can transfer a future right immediately; words of the future alone (bare promise) are generally insufficient for a free gift unless accompanied by other signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of Contract — By Inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs by Inference arise from words, silence, actions, or forbearing an action — anything that sufficiently argues the will of the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context such as conduct or silence can be interpreted as indication of intent to transfer; what suffices is what reasonably demonstrates the will to contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free Gift Passes by Words of the Present or Past (but not bare future promises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of present or past time can pass a free gift (e.g., 'I have given' or 'I do give to be delivered tomorrow'). Bare future promises (e.g., 'I will give tomorrow') are insufficient to transfer a free gift unless accompanied by other signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes different verbal forms: 'I will that this be thine tomorrow' (present act of will) versus 'I will give it to thee tomorrow' (promise of future act). Examples: offering a prize or throwing money publicly may make a future-form word effective because other signs accompany it.

rubrics_metrics.name: In Contracts a Promise is Equivalent to a Covenant
rubrics_metrics.description: When contract is mutual and one party promises because he has already received the benefit, the promise is to be understood as intending transfer; in buying and selling, promise is equivalent to covenant and therefore obligatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A promise that induces performance by the other party is treated as binding because the performer relies on it; in commerce promises have binding force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit: Performance First Entitles to Due
rubrics_metrics.description: He that performs first in a contract 'merits' that which he is to receive and has it as due. In prizes or thrown money (free gifts contested by event), the winner merits and may claim the prize as due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes merit in contract (owed by other contractor) from merit in gratuitous contests (owed by the benignity of the giver). Scholastic distinction between meritum congrui and meritum condigni discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants of Mutual Trust are Invalid in the State of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: If a covenant requires neither party to perform immediately but trusts mutual future performance, in the condition of mere Nature (state of war) it is void upon any reasonable suspicion because the performer has no assurance the other will perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only where a common power exists capable of compelling performance are such covenants valid. Fear of coercive power is the necessary backing in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to the End Includes Right to the Means
rubrics_metrics.description: He that transfers any right transfers the means of enjoying it, as far as lies in his power (e.g., selling land transfers herbage; selling a mill implies not diverting the stream).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfer of jurisdiction or sovereign rights implies transfer of power to levy money, maintain soldiers, appoint magistrates necessary to the exercise of that right.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Covenant with Brute Beasts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to make covenant with brute beasts because they do not understand speech and cannot accept translation of right; without mutual acceptance there is no covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual understanding and acceptance are necessary for covenants; animals lack the capacity for mutual contractual acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Covenant with God without Special Revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: To make covenant with God is impossible except by mediation of those to whom God speaks (revelation) or his lieutenants; otherwise we do not know whether our covenants are accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vows contrary to law of nature are vain; if commanded by law of nature, the law, not the vow, binds. Religious form of oath relies on recognized mediation/authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Covenant Except About Possible and Future Things
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of a covenant is always something deliberated, therefore something to come and judged possible for the promiser to perform. To promise the impossible is no covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If performance becomes impossible after making the covenant, the covenant remains valid binding to the value or to sincere effort to perform as much as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants are Discharged by Performance or Forgiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are freed of their covenants either by performing them or by being forgiven; performance is the natural end of obligation, forgiveness is the restitution of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the two ordinary ways obligations end; forgiveness is conceptualized as retransferring the right in which the obligation consisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants Extorted by Fear Are Valid
rubrics_metrics.description: Covenants entered into by fear (e.g., paying ransom for life) in the condition of mere nature are obligatory: one receives benefit of life and the other receives payment or service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prisoners of war obliged to pay ransom; coerced bargains for survival are binding unless later civil law discharges them. Fear that lawfully allows action can also lawfully bind the promiser.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Former Covenant Makes Void a Later Covenant Over the Same Right
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man has already passed away his right to one man, he has not that same right to pass to another; therefore the later promise passes no right and is null.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal priority of transfer establishes which covenant is effective; rights already transferred cannot be transferred again.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Covenant Not to Defend Oneself is Void
rubrics_metrics.description: A covenant not to defend oneself from force by force is always void because nobody can transfer the right to save himself from death, wounds, or imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promises of non-resistance in face of lethal force transfer no right and are not binding; this underlies the practice of using armed men even when a condemned criminal consents to execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Man Obliged to Accuse Himself
rubrics_metrics.description: A covenant to accuse oneself without assurance of pardon is invalid because in the state of nature there is no place for accusation, and in the civil state accusation is followed by punishment which is force and may be resisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accusations extracted by torture are unreliable and should not be credited; the right of self-preservation allows false or true accusation under duress as escape from danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Oath: Form and Function
rubrics_metrics.description: An oath is a form of speech added to a promise by which the promiser signifies that unless he performs he renounces God's mercy or calls God to vengeance on himself; oaths are used to strengthen covenants by invoking fear of divine vengeance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oaths must be taken according to the swearer's religion to be effective; swearing by what one does not consider God is vain. The greatest binding power is fear of human punishment in civil society, but in state of nature fear of invisible powers (religion) may be all that can strengthen a covenant.

rubrics_metrics.name: An Oath Adds Nothing to Obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: An oath adds nothing to obligation: a lawful covenant binds before an oath as much as after; an unlawful covenant is not made binding by an oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The oath operates psychologically (fear of divine vengeance) but does not create new moral or legal obligation beyond an already lawful covenant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Law of Nature: Justice (Keep Covenants)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the law commanding transfer of rights that hinder peace follows the Third: That men perform their covenants made; without which covenants are in vain and the right of all men to all things would remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice is identified with performance of covenants; failure to perform is injustice. The origin of justice is thus contractual and tied to commonwealth formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice and Injustice Defined
rubrics_metrics.description: In this law of nature consists the origin of JUSTICE: where no covenant has preceded there is no right transferred and no action can be unjust. When a covenant is made, to break it is UNJUST. INJUSTICE defined as the not-performance of covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice applies only where covenants and property (propriety) have been established; otherwise 'just' and 'unjust' have no application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice Requires a Commonwealth (Coercive Power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before names of Just and Unjust have place there must be some coercive power to compell men to perform their covenants; property and propriety begin with constitution of a civil power sufficient to compel performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a commonwealth and coercive punishment greater than temptation to breach, covenants are not valid; justice as keeping covenant presupposes social enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice is Not Contrary to Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping of covenant (justice) is a rule of reason, forbidding anything destructive to life; arguments that successful wickedness could be reasonable are refuted: breach of faith undermines one's ability to be part of society and to preserve life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if breaking a covenant could yield a benefit, it is against reason because it jeopardizes the security granted by others and undermines one's future prospects of peaceful association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants Not Discharged by the Vice of the Person to Whom Made
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that the other party has a faulty character (heretiques or habitual breakers) does not in reason discharge our covenant; if that fault was sufficient to discharge it, it should have prevented the making of the covenant in the first place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejects exceptions that would render covenants unstable based on perceived character of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice of Men vs Justice of Actions
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'just' and 'unjust' are attributed to men they signify conformity of manners to reason; when attributed to actions they signify conformity to reason of particular acts. A just man strives to make his actions just; an unjust man neglects that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A righteous man does not lose title by a few unjust actions from passion or error; labels of 'guiltless' apply to actions, while 'righteous' applies to disposition. Distinction clarifies moral evaluation of persons and acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing Done to a Man by His Own Consent Can Be Injury
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is done conformable to a man's own will signified to the doer is no injury to him; if he has not passed away originall right by antecedent covenant, there's no breach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent negates injury; if prior covenant existed, a signified will is a release of that covenant and thus no injury results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutative and Distributive Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice of actions is divided into Commutative (equality in exchange/contract — arithmetic proportion) and Distributive (distribution of equal benefit to men of equal merit — geometric proportion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commutative justice relates to contractors and performance of contractual obligations (buying, selling, hiring, lending). Distributive justice more properly called equity — the act of an arbitrator assigning each his due.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth Law of Nature: Gratitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Gratitude depends on antecedent grace (free-gift): 'That a man which receiveth benefit from another of meer Grace, endeavour that he which giveth it, have no reasonable cause to repent him of his good will.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breach of this law is ingratitude and threatens the beginning of benevolence and mutual help necessary to end the state of war and seek peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth Law of Nature: Mutual Accommodation (Compleasance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man should strive to accommodate himself to the rest; because diversity of aptness to society means some persons' asperities hinder building a stable society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to stones in building: those whose stubborn passions take more room than they fill are cast out as troublesome; mutual accommodation is necessary to maintain social cooperation.
